samples.question: Two bordered boards appear here, one on the left and one taller and narrower on the right, with a wide stretch of empty backdrop between them; faint grey shapes lying beyond both borders belong to the backdrop and should be ignored entirely. The left board is an allowance sheet of four rows. A row shows a large disc of one colour, and beside it, to its right, a group of one, two or three small dark dots. Each of the four rows uses a different colour, and the dot group tells you that colour's allowance: the number of parcels of that colour that must still be handed in. Only how many dots there are counts; how they are laid out does not, and neither does which row happens to be printed above which. The right board is a chute. Thin dark rules divide it into twelve compartments in a single column, and every compartment holds one smaller disc. The compartment at the very top holds the parcel that is handed in first, the one below it the parcel handed in second, and so on down to the bottom compartment, which is handed in last. Hand the parcels in one by one in that order. Every parcel handed in reduces the allowance of its own colour by exactly one, and a colour's allowance is used up at the instant the number of its parcels handed in so far first equals its printed dot count. The chute always contains three parcels of each of the four colours and no allowance exceeds three, so all four allowances do get used up in the end; parcels are handed in one at a time, so one colour necessarily gets there before any other. The boards are not pinned to fixed spots, and the four colours in use are always teal, violet, orange and moss. Whose allowance is used up first? Answer with one of teal, violet, orange or moss.
